I've been teaching Personal Protection classes (mandatory for CCW permits in a few states where I've lived) for about 14 years now. Never shot a gun? You need some Professional instruction. It is the Fastest way to gaining proficiency, while not picking up any bad habits that can screw you in the end. Along the way you'll learn basic safety, get comfortable shooting (we used 22lr pistols to help teach the Techniques without the issues of a centerfire, lots of people who are timid/unsure at first), try out a bunch of different styles, get your hands on all sorts of different pistols, etc... you may find that a revolver is right for you vs a semi-auto (smaller, easier to conceal, reliable like a hammer, and personally I'm Far more accurate in high pressure/short time situations ~ the obvious downside is reloading/rounds available).

But get education. Then look at budget, and finally shoot the options you can afford. There aren't really any Bad firearms for sale these days, but it'll never hurt to stick with a major name brand. Buy what feels best in your hand, and what you're comfortable shooting. A .357 that you're not proficient with is more of a hindrance than a .22lr that you have the utmost confidence in. And lest you be concerned about the effectiveness of .22lr, it's the round with the most deaths attributed every year (mostly because they are SO prevalent and easy to shoot, but a well placed 22lr will one-shot-stop someone as well as any hand cannon you can think of).

The most important aspect of the class I'm suggesting though, is learning situational awareness... how to avoid and prevent the need to rely upon a weapon. A pistol needs to be Absolute last option, after exhausting everything else, or you are going to be torn to shreds in court. You know what happens when people like us go to court, right? What Gardening Method Do You Use?

This year I'll experiment with a tiered hydroponics system. After converting my patio to a (fairly small) attached greenhouse I noticed that there just wasn't enough room to grow everything. I have too darn many seeds and only room enough for about 10 or 15 plants.

The solution to that is to go vertical. Yes, I could build a tiered rack of some kind but I'd have trouble reaching some of the plants, especially those next to the polycarbonate walls and those at the top tier. So I had to think of a way to use the vertical space while still being able to reach all the plants for pruning, harvesting, etc.

The solution I came up with is a stacked tier hydroponics setup. I'll build it myself because I'm cheap and also because none of the commercially available products would allow me to take maximum advantage of the entire space. Some were too small, wasting space. Some were too big and outside my budget anyway, no help there. So I decided on a metal framework using pipes and pipe fittings, I wanted it to be adjustable so each tier could be raised or lowered but that's not really a necessity. Here's a side view, just to give you an idea of the layout.

 XX
 XX
 XX
 XX
 XX

Each "XX" represents a hydroponic trough. Water comes in at the near end and drains out at the far end. Each trough is removable to make harvesting easier and for cleaning if that is ever needed.

The water containment fits underneath nicely and I put hydroponic nutrients in there as well, watering and feeding the plants at the same time. Inside the nutrient tank is a water pump on a timer which pumps the water + nutrient solution to each tier.

I don't know if it will be a success or a disaster. It is an experiment so the outcome is unknown as of yet. But that's the exciting part about gardening, isn't it?
